title: Sh-M
hookLine: shem, a name, gives Exodus its Hebrew title, Shemot

lines: A TEACHER GUESSES AT A NAME.
EXODUS OPENS WITH A ROLL CALL.
cards: Roll call, first morning of school. The teacher reaches a name she has never seen, pauses, and takes a guess. The whole room turns to look at the kid whose name it is.
Will they correct her, or let it slide all year?
The second book of the Torah opens with a roll call of its own: "Now these are the names of the children of Israel, which came into Egypt; every man and his household came with Jacob."
The book is about to tell how a family was put to hard labor under taskmasters. Before any of that, it says their names.

teach.b: Sh-M. Two letters, shin and mem. Shem: a name.
The second book takes its Hebrew title from that opening verse: Shemot, names. English calls it Exodus, the way out; Hebrew calls it the names. First, the roll call.

Genesis already listed these same sons going down to Egypt, so why again? The medieval commentator Rashi answers: to show how dear they are, the way God brings out the stars by number and calls each one by name.
A midrash adds that the people were redeemed, in part, because they did not change their names.
Second, a name for God that works by not being a name. You met the burning bush back in year one: Moses asks what name to give the people, and hears "I AM THAT I AM."
Today some Jews, in everyday speech, call God simply Hashem: the Name. It's a way of speaking of God with care, without saying the holy name lightly. Third, a name you build.
Ecclesiastes says, "A good name is better than precious ointment."

teach.h: A GOOD NAME OVER GOOD OIL.
teach.b: The Hebrew is a pun: tov shem mi-shemen tov, a good shem over good shemen, oil. Perfume fades by evening. The name you earn stays in the room after you leave.

Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. To say someone's name properly is to tell them they're a person, not a number on a list. That's what the first verse of Shemot does for a family about to be worked as labor.

how: The Hebrew title of Exodus is Shemot, names, from its opening verse; some Jews speak of God as Hashem, the Name, and Jewish teaching prizes a shem tov, a good name, which Pirkei Avot sets above the crowns of Torah, priesthood and kingship.

games.q: you're one of Jacob's family in Egypt, far from home, under hard masters. a midrash asks what you held on to. what is it?
o: you take Egyptian names so you'll fit in.
you keep the names you were given.
you stop using names at all.
games.why: the midrash teaches that the people were redeemed, in part, because they did not change their names.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose name you've been saying a little wrong, or never quite caught, a coworker or a neighbor, and plan the simple question: I want to get your name right, how do you say it?
Then let the names of people you love pass through your mind slowly, one at a time, the way the book of names begins. If you pray, you can hold each one before God as it comes.
